QF.id: VIII Introduction to Forwards and Futures_40

question.text: Which of the following is the MOST accurate statement about the relationship between forward and futures prices for the same underlying and expiry?

answer.text: In theory, forward and futures prices should be identical for the same underlying and expiry if interest rates are constant, but daily marking-to-market of futures can create minor differences
Futures prices are always higher than forward prices because futures have the additional cost of exchange fees
Forward prices are always higher than futures prices because forwards have counterparty risk premium
There is no theoretical relationship between forward and futures prices; they are determined by entirely different market forces

explanation.text: The Logic: The standard derivatives-pricing result (Cox, Ingersoll, Ross) is that when interest rates are deterministic / constant, the forward price and the futures price for the same underlying and same expiry are equal. When interest rates are stochastic, daily marking-to-market on futures changes the timing of cash flows: futures gains/losses are realised and reinvested (or funded) day by day, so the futures price can differ slightly from the forward price depending on the correlation between the underlying and interest rates. The Trap: Futures are not always higher than forwards because of exchange fees, nor are forwards always higher because of counterparty risk — those are real-world frictions, not the theoretical pricing relationship. And there IS a theoretical relationship between the two prices; they are not driven by unrelated market forces. Note: The cited NISM Series VIII Equity Derivatives workbook covers no-arbitrage futures pricing, forward-vs-futures contract differences and daily MTM mechanics, but the pages checked do not explicitly state the equivalence result under constant rates or attribute minor forward-futures price differences to daily MTM. The framing above is general derivatives-pricing theory.
